title: Serving the nagar kirtan
hookLine: families serve food and water along the procession route
tomorrow: it's June, it's hot, and a stranger hands you a free drink. why?

lines: IS THIS GETTING OUT OF HAND?
cards: On a nagar kirtan route, it starts with folding tables. Families set them up along the sidewalk: steel pots, coolers, paper plates, a banner with the family's name.
By noon, someone walking the route can be handed pakoras, fruit, juice, chai, ice cream, a full plate of rice and dal. Free, to anyone.
And every year, somewhere in the sangat, someone asks out loud: is this getting out of hand?

teach.h: THE CASE FOR PLENTY: MATA KHIVI'S KHEER.
teach.b: That question is a real conversation among Sikhs, and both sides have a strong case. The case for plenty first. Langar has a generous history.
In the Ramkali ki Var, the bards Satta and Balvand praise Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife, whose langar served rich kheer made with ghee.

Serving the road with plenty says: in the Guru's house nobody leaves hungry, and nobody is too poor for the good food. Families who have served the same corner for years feel it as their seva, and their joy.

teach.h: THE CASE FOR SIMPLE: KEEP THE CENTER.
teach.b: Now the case for simple. Some sangats and Sikh writers ask for fewer stalls and simpler food: less plastic, less waste, less of a food fair. Their point is the center.
A nagar kirtan is kirtan: the Guru Granth Sahib carried through town with the sangat singing behind. If the crowd follows the dessert tables, the Guru passes by unnoticed.
And one thing both sides already share is the road itself.

teach.h: BOTH SWEEP AHEAD OF THE PALKI.
teach.b: Volunteers walk ahead of the palki, sweeping and washing the street, so the Guru travels a clean path.
Whatever ends up on the tables, the serving starts with a broom.

how: Along a nagar kirtan route, Sikh families and gurdwara groups set up stalls handing out free food and drinks to anyone passing; volunteers sweep the road ahead of the Guru Granth Sahib, and some sangats now organize cleanup and less disposable ware.

games.q: what does “serving the nagar kirtan” mean?
o: marching at the front with the Guru Granth Sahib
serving food, water and cleanup along the procession
selling food at stalls to fund the gurdwara

games.q: two cases, one road — tap the pairs.
p: her langar served kheer made with ghee
keep the Guru and the kirtan at the center
the bards of the Ramkali ki Var

s: Sikh teaching says rich food has no place in langar
the Ramkali ki Var praises Mata Khivi's langar for kheer made with ghee.
volunteers sweep the road ahead of the Guru Granth Sahib
the road is readied so the Guru travels a clean path.
the food stalls are the main point of a nagar kirtan
the center is kirtan: the Guru Granth Sahib carried through town, the sangat singing.

games.q: your youth group is split. you want a big menu: samosas, ice cream, the works. Jas wants water and one simple dish. state Jas's best case.
o: the procession is kirtan; simpler tables keep the Guru at the center and cut the waste.
simple food is holier; rich food goes against Sikh teaching.
big stalls are showing off, and people only serve to be seen.
games.why: the simple side isn't against good food: Mata Khivi's langar served kheer with ghee. its case is the center, the Guru passing and the sangat singing. both sides serve the road.

practice: Sit up and hold both hands out in front of you, palms up, as if offering a cup to someone walking past. Stay in that posture for the sit, breathing slowly.
Notice what it's like to keep your hands open with no idea who the next person will be.

wordCard.voice: Serving the nagar kirtan. Setting up along the procession route to feed, water and clean up after it: seva done on the street, for anyone.

orig.note: Punjabi: nagar, a town; kirtan, singing the Guru's hymns. the hymns carried through the town.

carryVoice: Something to keep: serve the road, the people on it and the street beneath them. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ramkali ki Var, Satta and Balvand, pauri 3 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967: Mata Khivi's langar, kheer with ghee), paraphrased
Sikh practice: nagar kirtan, route stalls, and sweeping the road ahead of the palki
Contemporary Sikh discussion of simpler nagar kirtan stalls and less waste (some sangats and writers)
